title: Industrial Property Identification
name: Industrial Property Identification
metaTitle: Industrial Property Identification in Los Angeles, CA
metaDescription: Sourcing port-adjacent and infill industrial replacement candidates in Los Angeles County against real clear-height, dock, and truck-court specs.

sections.html:
Industrial replacement candidates near the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach get evaluated on a narrower set of specs than most other asset classes, clear height, dock door count, truck court depth, and power capacity, and that narrower spec sheet is exactly why so few buildings actually qualify as strong candidates. We identify against those specs directly rather than against a general size and price range, since two buildings of similar square footage can be miles apart in functional value once clear height and truck maneuvering room are factored in.

We document each candidate's specs on a standardized sheet before any comparison happens, so an exchanger reviewing several options at once is judging them against the same measured criteria rather than against a broker's marketing description.

sections.heading: Why Infill Industrial Is the Scarcest Product Type in the County
sections.html:
Land available for new industrial construction in the corridor stretching from Vernon and Commerce through the City of Industry has been effectively built out for years, which means most available inventory is existing product rather than new construction, and vacancy on well-specified buildings rarely lasts long. A functional building with 28-foot or higher clear height and a real truck court, not a shared lot, can draw multiple offers within days of listing, and an exchanger's 45-day identification window offers no cushion for a search that starts from scratch after a relinquished sale closes.

We track available and off-market industrial inventory across this corridor continuously, not only when an active exchange requires it, so a candidate list can be assembled from properties already reviewed rather than a cold search under deadline pressure.

We also keep a working list of off-market owners who have indicated a willingness to sell under the right terms, since some of the strongest industrial buildings in this corridor never formally list, and an exchanger relying only on active listings is working from a smaller pool than what actually exists.

sections.heading: The Spec Sheet We Actually Screen Against
sections.html:
• Clear height, with anything under 24 feet ruled out for most modern distribution use
  • Number and configuration of dock-high doors relative to building depth
  • Truck court depth sufficient for trailer maneuvering, beyond simple parking
  • Power capacity, particularly for candidates suited to light manufacturing or cold storage conversion
  • Rail access or proximity, relevant for a narrower set of industrial users

sections.heading: Where Environmental Review Adds Time the 180-Day Clock Does Not Forgive
sections.html: Older industrial buildings in this corridor, particularly those with a history of manufacturing or fuel storage use, often need a Phase I environmental site assessment before a lender will finalize financing, and a Phase I that surfaces a recommendation for further investigation can add weeks to a closing timeline. We flag environmental risk on any candidate before it is placed on the identification list, since discovering a Phase II requirement on day 100 of a 180-day exchange leaves very little room to recover.

sections.heading: Tenant Quality and Lease Structure on In-Place Industrial
sections.html: Most available industrial candidates in this market come with an existing tenant in place, and the quality of that lease, term remaining, renewal options, and whether rent reflects current market rather than a stale legacy rate, matters as much as the physical building specs. We review lease abstracts on every serious candidate before identification, since a building with strong specs but a tenant paying well under market carries a different near-term cash flow profile than the asking price alone would suggest.

sections.heading: Matching Candidates to the Exchanger's Actual Hold Strategy
sections.html:
An exchanger looking for stable in-place income wants a different candidate than one planning to hold through a lease expiration and reposition the building for a higher-paying tenant, and we sort the candidate pool by that distinction before presenting it, rather than handing over every available listing that meets the physical spec threshold. Matching the property to the strategy up front avoids identifying a candidate that technically qualifies but does not fit what the exchanger actually intends to do with it.

We put this comparison in writing before identification, listing each shortlisted candidate against the exchanger's stated hold strategy, so the final identification decision is made against a documented comparison rather than a verbal impression formed during a property tour.

faqs.q: Why is infill industrial harder to find than other Los Angeles asset classes?
faqs.a: The corridor near the ports has little available land for new construction, so most inventory is existing product, and well-specified buildings with strong clear height and dock access rarely stay on the market long.

faqs.q: What clear height is generally needed for a strong industrial candidate?
faqs.a: Most modern distribution and light industrial use benefits from at least 24 to 28 feet of clear height. Buildings below that threshold are typically ruled out early in the screening process.

faqs.q: How does environmental review affect industrial exchange timing?
faqs.a: A Phase I assessment that recommends further investigation can add weeks to closing, which is why we flag environmental risk on any candidate before it is placed on the identification list.

faqs.q: Does an existing tenant's lease rate matter for identification purposes?
faqs.a: Yes. A tenant paying well under current market rent changes the near-term cash flow profile of a candidate even if the physical building specs are strong, so we review lease terms before identification.

faqs.q: Can rail access be a meaningful differentiator among industrial candidates?
faqs.a: For a narrower set of industrial users, yes, though it is not a requirement for most distribution and light manufacturing tenants in this market.
